subject: Chemistry
title: Wine: Grapes to Alcohol
description: A quick win: understand Wine: Grapes to Alcohol.

hook.text: Wine is grape juice transformed by yeast. The yeast eats sugar and produces ethanol—and 1,000 flavor compounds.

buildup.text: Grape juice contains 15–25% sugar. Yeast ferments it over weeks, converting sugar to alcohol and CO₂.

discovery.text: Fermentation stops when alcohol reaches about 15%—the yeast poisons itself with its own waste product.

twist.text: Red wine gets its color from grape skin contact during fermentation. White wine is fermented without skins.

climax.text: Aging in oak barrels adds vanillin (vanilla) and tannins. The barrel chemistry is as important as the grape.

punchline.text: Yeast eats sugar, makes alcohol, then dies in it. Wine is yeast's last meal.

quiz.question: Why does wine fermentation stop naturally around 15% alcohol?
options: The yeast is killed by the alcohol it produces
All the sugar has been consumed
Oxygen runs out in the sealed container

details.summary: Wine fermentation converts grape sugars to ethanol and carbon dioxide through yeast metabolism. The chemical complexity of wine comes from hundreds of secondary metabolites including terpenes for aroma, anthocyanins for color, tannins for astringency, and esters for fruity notes.
details.whyItMatters: Winemaking is a multi-billion dollar industry built on fermentation chemistry. Understanding wine chemistry enables consistent quality production and has advanced microbiology, enzymology, and organic chemistry.
takeaways: Yeast converts grape glucose and fructose to ethanol and carbon dioxide
Hundreds of secondary compounds create wine's complex flavor profile
Aging in oak barrels adds vanillin, lactones, and tannin compounds

faq.question: Why do different grape varieties produce wines with such different flavors?
faq.answer: Each grape variety has a unique genetic profile that determines its terpene, thiol, anthocyanin, and phenolic compound concentrations. These secondary metabolites, combined with soil minerals, climate effects, and specific yeast strain interactions, create distinct flavor fingerprints.

faq.question: What chemical changes occur during wine aging that improve flavor?
faq.answer: Tannins polymerize into larger, softer molecules. Esters form through slow acid-alcohol reactions, adding fruity complexity. Oxygen slowly penetrates the cork, enabling controlled oxidation reactions. Harsh young compounds transform into smoother, more complex molecules over years.
